item.title: The Republican Strategy to Salvage the Midterms
item.description:
With Republicans trailing in the polls, the party is making hard choices about where to spend its money — abandoning some races while pouring resources into others.

Shane Goldmacher, Nate Cohn and Lisa Lerer, political correspondents for The New York Times, explain why President Trump is campaigning almost daily in deep-red territory, how his influence is shaping the strategy and whether Democrats can win over the disenchanted voters they may need to take back the House and the Senate.

Guests: 

  • Shane Goldmacher, a national political correspondent for The New York Times.
  • Nate Cohn, the chief political analyst for The New York Times.
  • Lisa Lerer, a national political correspondent for The New York Times.

Background reading: 

  • Economic pain and an unpopular Trump have put the G.O.P. on its heels.
  • Top Republican groups are pulling support from two House incumbents.

Photo: Kenny Holston/The New York Times

item.title: The U.S. Tried to Choke Russia’s Energy Market. Then It Made a Diesel Deal.
item.description:
President Trump announced a deal to purchase Russian diesel fuel and temporarily suspended sanctions in an effort to lower domestic fuel prices amid rising costs from the war in Iran and in anticipation of the upcoming midterms. This abrupt foreign policy shift stunned European allies and drew sharp criticism from Ukraine, which viewed the move as a weakening of Western leverage against Russia.

Today, Anton Troianovski, a global affairs correspondent for The New York Times, discusses what the deal reveals about the Trump administration’s strategy with Russia, and how much it could actually lower prices at the pump.

Guest: Anton Troianovski, a global affairs correspondent for The New York Times who writes about foreign policy, national security and America’s place in the world.

Background reading: Trump faces a new crisis over Ukraine following the Russian diesel deal.

Photo: Igor Grussak/picture alliance via Getty Images

item.title: When A.I. Comes for Your Purpose in Life
item.description:
Artificial intelligence has gone from struggling with basic arithmetic to helping solve some of mathematics’ most famous open problems — and the field is reckoning with what that means.

Steven Strogatz, a professor of mathematics at Cornell University, describes the excitement and grief of watching A.I. take on work that gives people a sense of purpose — and asks what could be lost if machines deliver answers without the human struggle, insight and understanding that make solving problems meaningful.

Guest: Steven Strogatz, a professor of mathematics at Cornell University who writes for The New York Times about the future of research.

Background reading: 

  • Mathematics isn’t just a game to let A.I. solve — history shows why.
  • A.I. is mastering the kinds of projects that have long helped to build the careers of young mathematicians. What does that mean for their future?
  • Steven Strogatz’s forthcoming book: Big Math.

Photo: Ian C. Bates for The New York Times
